“Churros! Hot churros!”
“Two for five! Tamales!”
“¡Cincuenta centavos más! ¡No me grites!”
There was noise layered over noise over more noise. Even fish markets in India couldn’t compete.
A dozen pairs of sunken eyes looked up at her from the sidewalk, spent syringes scattered around the pavement like matchsticks. She tightened her grip on the suitcase handles.
*“JESUS IS OUR SAVIOR!”*

An old man was screaming into a crackling megaphone, his hands slicing through the air like an orchestra conductor’s. “Our Father has sent the Son as Savior of the world. He died for your sins and rose again. Let the Lord’s light touch your face! Do you know Jesus loves you?”

Riya turned in a slow circle. Every wall she could see was covered in color. An alley half a block up ran mural to mural, painted with faces the size of doors. Street vendors were hawking knockoff sunglasses and freshly cut mango slices, the air thick with the smell of fried food and gasoline. Cars honked endlessly, stuck behind buses that exhaled like exhausted animals.
Just as she stepped off the curb, someone slammed into her shoulder.
“Watch it!”
The wheel of her suitcase got lodged in a BART grate and twisted with a sickening crack. She yanked it free, dragging the thing across the street in a hurry before the light turned green.

The Friday afternoon sun hung low, casting long, jagged shadows across the pavement hot enough to be a griddle. Sweat slid down the back of her neck. Strands of hair plastered themselves to her forehead. This wasn’t the welcome she’d imagined, but surely it could only go up—
“*Shit!*”

Not an expletive, though it might as well have been. A fresh splatter of white droppings bloomed across her red suitcase. She looked up just in time to see the culprit. A soaring pigeon, flying away guilt-free into a cloudless San Francisco sky.

Thirty minutes later, the broken wheel whining against pavement, her shoulders burning, the streets softened into rows of two- and three-story Victorians. Laundry flapped from rusted balconies, and a few houses had eviction notices taped to the doors, fluttering like tired flags.
“1069… 1071… 1073…” she muttered. Then, finally: “1075.”

The house looked like it belonged to a different decade. A three-story Edwardian, faded seafoam green, its façade blotchy from layers of repaint and years of city soot. The windows bulged outward like eyes that had seen too much.

She climbed the porch steps and plopped down, breathless. Save for a sparrow’s chirrup, the place felt deserted. She was exhausted, hungry, and suddenly unsure. What had she done? This was not the city of jugglers in business suits. While reaching for her phone, her hands brushed against the ticket stub for the *Echo Sounds* concert. She looked at it for a long time, then let out a laugh, unable to believe that this stupid piece of paper had set off a chain reaction that uprooted her whole life.
*“is that you down there?”*

Riya looked up from the porch steps. Felix’s pale face appeared in the second-story window like a magic trick. She waved, and quickly tried to tame her hair. Smile, she lectured herself, and don’t look overwhelmed.
The door creaked open, but it wasn’t Felix. A tall, shirtless man appeared, holding a mason jar.
“Welcome,” he said, his smile barely touching his lips. “I’m Paul.”
“Hi Paul!”
He held the door as she wrestled her defaced suitcases inside. Felix was leaning against the stairwell banister, linen pants and a vintage Prince t-shirt completing the portrait.
“I’m impressed, Riya,” he said. “You actually did it.”

He walked over and pulled her into a longer hug. Despite feeling unclean and sticky from dragging a hundred pounds through heat that clung to her skin, she stepped forward to receive it like a giddy passenger heading into first class for the first time.
“Come on,” he said, turning toward the stairs. “Let me give you a tour.”

Paul had already disappeared. She started hauling her suitcases up the stairs but stopped midway. The walls along the stairs were covered in strange, beautiful things: giant charts mapping the origin of religion, a framed chart of the thirty cognitive biases, a sprawling mess of hand-drawn art—much of it bodies with no clothes on—and a picture of five people in a tiny ball pit. A battered piano sat quietly in the upstairs hallway, two of its keys taped with smiley faces. She inspected it all like it was the Museum of Modern Art.
“Five people from five countries live here,” Felix said, watching her. “With you, we’re six from six. A perfect little United Nations of Chaos.”

Upstairs, the house smelled of incense and unwashed dishes. Felix swept his arms at a 12-by-12-foot living room cluttered with three oddly shaped couches, a wooden dining table, and a projector screen. It felt like stepping into someone’s brain.
“This is where the fun happens,” Felix said. “The stage for our salons, parties, movie nights, obstacle courses… You name it.”
“Obstacle courses?”
“You’ll see.” Felix winked. “Inaya lives in the room downstairs. Grace and Paul are on this floor with you. Om and I live upstairs.”

A petite woman emerged from the kitchen. Fair, thin, black hair, and big eyes for a tiny face. Her arms were stretched, reaching forward like she was hugging her long-lost cousin. “Riya! I’m Grace. You must be exhausted.”
Riya smiled, hugging her back, immediately feeling the warmth.
Felix cleared his throat. “Let me show you your room.”

He turned and slid open what Riya had assumed was a closet, or maybe the laundry space. Instead, it was her room. It didn’t have a lock, or a proper door, just a carved-out section likely used as the dining room when the house wasn’t taken over by the United Nations of Chaos. The old hardwood floor creaked, and dust piled in the corners. A deflated air mattress was on the ground next to a folded blanket. A naked bulb dangled from the ceiling. The window didn’t offer much of a view—just the side of another house—but it let in light, and the breeze rustled the curtain gently, as if whispering hello.
“I gotta get back.” Felix backed toward the staircase. “But tell me if you need something.”
She needed everything, right from a mattress to a door lock to some reassurance that the invitation under the lemon tree had meant something. But for now, all she really needed was water.

Like most of the house, the kitchen was tiny, barely enough space for three to stand without butting heads. Grace was boiling tea, steam rising in gentle spirals. Riya hovered at the doorway, feeling the familiar temptation to retreat and wait till the coast was clear. It felt odd to step into a kitchen with another person.
“Grace,” she said, steadying her voice. “Do you mind if I cook for you all tonight?”
“Really?” Grace turned around. “Because I *love* Indian food! Especially Chicken Tikka Masala. I once had it at this gorgeous little restaurant in Toronto. Oh wait, I’m sorry, are you Indian?”
Riya laughed. “Yes, but I am vegetarian. How about I make lentil stew instead?”
Grace grinned. “You’re officially hired.”

Riya propped her phone against the spice rack and scanned a recipe, moving quickly enough to look like she’d done it a hundred times before. The cabinet was missing half the spices she needed, so she improvised, tipping what she could find into the modern-day cauldron, an Instant Pot. Meanwhile, Grace chopped onions and peppered her with questions: how was Des Moines, how she met Felix, what was her favorite book. Riya answered them lightly, smiling and nodding, while her brain raced ahead of her hands.
Felix and Paul had vanished back into their workdays, and Grace followed suit after the chopping, leaving her alone in the kitchen.

Riya gripped the counter and let her shoulders drop. The adrenaline that had carried her across the country drained all at once. Her calves throbbed from dragging the broken suitcase uphill. Why did she choose to only sleep three hours the night before? For a second, she considered sliding down to the floor and closing her eyes.
Instead, she straightened.

To distract herself, she looked around and noticed the details that made the house feel alive: a pickle jar labeled OM JAR above the fridge, a collage of postcards and curling notes on the door, and, behind the blender, a small label-maker sticker that read: *not a cult*. Just below it, in French: *pas un culte.* That made her chuckle.
After cleaning up, she stood in the middle of her dusty bedroom, listening to the soft hum of the pressure cooker and the distant strumming of someone’s guitar upstairs.

She rolled up her sleeves and spent the next hour cleaning, wiping, sweeping, scrubbing, and pushing the deflated mattress into the center of the room.Clothes, toiletries, books. Most of her life was contained in those two suitcases, half-splayed open on the floor. She lined her books along the wall carefully. By the time she was done, the room still looked empty, but a little less anonymous.

When the cooker fell silent, she went back to the kitchen and began setting the table, fumbling around for plates, mugs, and utensils. None of the plates matched each other. She walked past the kitchen in search of Grace and Paul’s rooms. There was only one door, though. When she knocked, Grace opened it halfway with Paul sitting behind her on the bed.
“We’ll be right there,” Grace said, signaling she was on a call.

Riya was surprised at the flutter in her stomach. She hadn’t eaten with people—*really* eaten with people—in years. It felt like the first day of school again. Tonight mattered more than she wanted to admit.

When she returned from the bathroom a few minutes later, someone new was already at the table. Shaggy dark brown hair fell into his eyes and headphones hung around his neck. He was serving himself with efficiency, as if he had done this a hundred times before.
She chirped, “Hi! I’m Riya.”
“Om,” he said, nodding once. “Thank you for the food.”
With that, he disappeared down the hallway. She was momentarily thrown off, but recovered quickly and slid into the center seat at the table.
Grace and Paul emerged from the kitchen.
“Welcome, guys,” Riya exclaimed. “I hope you like the food!”
“Of course we will,” Grace replied, sitting down next to her.
“Thanks,” Paul said, already adding rice onto his plate.
“So,” Riya said, leaning forward, “what do you guys do for work?”
“Well, I work as a marketing manager at a healthcare startup,” Grace said, spooning lentils. “Paul is the smarty pants. He’s an AI researcher at Google.”
“Wow,” Riya said. “What do you—”
“It’s eight already?”

Felix appeared in the doorway, barefoot, glancing once at his phone before slipping it into his back pocket. He slid into the seat beside her, close enough that their knees almost touched and shot her a sideways smile. She looked away quickly, tucking a strand of hair behind her ear as some kind of armor.
“What about you, Riya?” Grace asked.
“Huh?” Riya said, looking up. “What about me what?”
“What do *you* do?”
“Oh. I’m here to start a company,” she replied, realizing this was the first time she’d said it out loud to people. It felt electric.
“I smell cumin and capitalism.” Felix grinned. “Two of my favorite things.”
Riya smiled knowingly. She’d spent most of her twenty-fifth birthday diving into the case study of Felix Marlowe, the prodigy who built his first company at the age of eighteen.
“Did you know she can quote any dead guy?” Felix said, pointing to her. “Or girl. Go ahead. Test her.”
“Really?” Paul looked up, intrigued.
“Okay, okay, Obama!” Grace chimed in. “No, wait, that’s too easy. How about… Joni Mitchell?”
Riya cleared her throat. “‘Nobody ever said to Van Gogh, “Paint a Starry Night again, man.”’”
“Well, Joni Mitchell isn’t dead,” Paul pointed out dryly. He looked at Riya. “Virginia Woolf?”
Riya smirked. “‘Why are women so much more interesting to men than men are to women?’”
“Nice,” Felix said, approving.
“Hmm.” Paul murmured, his interest already fading.
“So, what’s your company about?” Grace asked, leaning in.
Riya exhaled. This was about to be her first pitch. If she couldn’t sell it to them over homemade lentil stew, she couldn’t sell it to anyone.

“It’s called Socratica,” she said, rubbing her hands beneath the table. “I mean, I’m calling it that for now. It’s about learning, basically. The way we *actually* learn, not the way we’re taught to. Right now, everything we consume just… disappears, doesn’t it? Even things from podcasts and videos. What if there was a way to make it all stay? To connect it, build on it, make it—”
The front door slammed. A woman with a green beanie and paint on her jeans dashed into the living room, waving a crumpled piece of paper like a flag of war.
“You will not *believe* this bullshit. They…” She noticed Riya and stopped. “Who’s this? Oh, are you Mia?”
“It’s, um, Riya. And you must be Inaya.”

Inaya’s eyes widened. “The Des Moines girl. Welcome. Sorry, I’m bad with names.” She dropped the crumpled paper onto the table like evidence. “So get this, Target docked me twenty-six minutes from my paycheck this week because I clocked in late two days in a row. Never mind that I stayed twenty-six minutes *after* shift to clean up a spill! I asked the manager about it, but he just shrugged and said, ‘It’s just system rounding.’ As if that’s a real answer. I should’ve told him, ‘If I rounded *you* down, you’d be headless.’”
Everyone laughed, except for Riya, who was still holding onto the thread of her idea.
“I’m sorry, honey,” Grace said, passing the food to Inaya. “Eat something.”
“Ugh.” Inaya plopped down. “Whatever, you know? Anyway, what brings you here?” She turned to Riya, finally noticing her properly.
“Riya was just telling us about her startup,” Grace said.
“Well, who isn’t?” Inaya rolled her eyes. “Seems like everyone you meet in SF has a weird startup idea.”
Riya felt a jab, but kept going.

“Yeah,” she said, clearing her throat. “Like I was saying, it’s about helping people learn differently. Right now, we mostly just… consume things. But what if it didn’t stop there? What if you could actually talk to the thing? Anyway, it’s kind of hard to explain.”
She reached for her water glass. Felix glanced at her sideways, just briefly, and she couldn’t tell if it was pity or something else.
“Have you raised funding yet?” he asked.
“Not yet,” she said. “That’s the next plan.”
“You know who raised funding for her crazy idea?” Inaya looked up suddenly from her phone. “River!”
“Seriously?” Paul asked, more alert now.

“Yuh-huh!” Inaya exclaimed. “She raised a *million* dollars for her Tarot app that generates daily digital cards based on, to quote her actual words, ‘planetary alignments and your digital footprint.’”
They all laughed, and Riya noticed Grace place her hand behind Paul’s neck, gently massaging it like she’d done it a hundred times before. Riya’s eyes lingered a moment too long.
Inaya continued, “Guys, she wore a bloody velvet cape to the pitch!”
“Brilliant,” Felix added. “She knew how to sell herself.”
Riya chimed in. “I read something about astrology apps—”
“Yeah, but this wasn’t even astrology,” Inaya cut in, animated now. “It’s like theater. She may as well have cast a spell on them.”

They laughed again. Riya reached for the water and let the conversation roll past her, nodding at the right moments, smiling when everyone else smiled, but quiet for the rest of it.Felix nudged her knee lightly under the table. She wasn’t sure if it was an accident, but he turned to look at her for a brief moment, nodding.

After dinner, Grace, Paul, and Inaya settled onto the sagging couch to watch *Psychokinesis*, a Korean film about a man who gains telekinetic powers and tries to reconnect with his estranged daughter. Riya would never have picked it, even in her strangest mood. She debated staying, but then saw Felix getting up to stretch and yawn.
“I’ve got a few things to finish up,” he said, already walking toward the stairs. “Goodnight, comrades.”
Riya watched him go, and after a moment, she too got up and retreated to her corner through the sliding doors.

Inside, she lay down on the still-deflated mattress, the blanket pulled up to her chin. The ceiling above her was cracked and yellowed in places. A cold breeze sneaked in through the window, even if it brought with it traffic noise. She stared ahead and thought about the pitch. *It’s kind of hard to explain.* She cringed. It wasn’t hard to explain. She’d written over ten thousand words about it. Tomorrow, she decided. She’d try again tomorrow.

It should’ve taken her a while to fall asleep with the laughter outside and the thud of someone dropping a pan. Inaya’s voice floated through, something about how kombucha is just witchcraft with better branding.
But she drifted off within minutes.
